title: Six sets of six
hook: the eye is not self, forms are not self, seeing is not self

segments.voice: Yesterday: Rahula awakens under a tree, and your line, all of it changing. Did you catch the eye changing while it looked? Today the same senses, counted out like beads. Day five hundred thirteen.

Thirty-six. That's how many items the hundred and forty-eighth discourse lays out, in six rows of six, like a spreadsheet of experience. It opens in Jeta's Grove at Savatthi with the Buddha announcing a teaching good in the beginning, good in the middle, good in the end. Then he simply counts. It can sound dry on the page, almost like an inventory. But the text itself says that while it was being spoken, the minds of sixty monks were freed. Today: six sets of six.
screen: `THIRTY-SIX ITEMS, SIX ROWS OF SIX.` → `JETA'S GROVE, SAVATTHI.` → `SIXTY MONKS FREED.`

segments.voice: Here are the six rows. First, the six inner bases: eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, mind. Second, the six outer bases: forms, sounds, smells, tastes, touches, and things known by the mind. Third, six kinds of consciousness, one for each meeting: seeing, hearing, and so on. Fourth, six kinds of contact, when sense, object and consciousness come together. Fifth, six kinds of feeling born of that contact. Sixth, six kinds of craving born of that feeling. Then comes the argument, and it's short. If anyone says the eye is self, the Buddha says, that doesn't hold. Why? Because the eye's arising and passing away are plainly seen. And if the eye were self, you'd have to say: my self arises and passes away. So the eye is not self. Then he runs the same test down the whole table. Forms: not self. Eye-consciousness: not self. Eye-contact, feeling, craving: not self. Thirty-six times, the same short proof. The Pali word is anatta, not-self. Notice what it doesn't say. It doesn't say nobody is here, or that nothing matters. It says that each piece you might point to and call me is something that comes and goes, so it can't be the permanent owner you were looking for. Then the discourse turns practical. When a pleasant feeling comes and you delight in it, a tendency toward lust is lying underneath. A painful one, and you resist it, aversion lies underneath. A neutral one, unnoticed, and ignorance lies underneath. Seeing all six rows clearly, the text says, a person grows disenchanted, and is freed.
screen: `SIX INNER, SIX OUTER` · `CONSCIOUSNESS, CONTACT, FEELING, CRAVING` · `IF THE EYE WERE SELF…` · `WHAT LIES UNDERNEATH A FEELING` · then, large: `NOT SELF, SIX TIMES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: check one sense for a self. Choose hearing. Close your eyes and let sounds come. A car. Your own breath. A hum. Now look for the one who owns the hearing. There's the sound. There's the ear. There's the hearing, arising and fading. Is there anything else, standing apart and permanent? Don't argue with yourself. Just look, and keep looking, gently. The bell holds the time.
Anatta. Not-self: thirty-six pieces of experience, each one arising and passing, so none of them the lasting self, tested row by row. Today's word.
Your line: not self, six times. Today, when a feeling seems to be all of you, notice it arrived through one of six doors, and it will leave. Day five hundred thirteen.

howItsDone: The six sense bases are a standard frame for insight meditation in Theravada practice; teachers often walk students through them one at a time, asking whether anything found there is lasting or can be called self.

fork.setup: someone tells you: the eye is my self. what does the Buddha in MN 148 point to?
options: the eye arises and passes away, so the self would too.
the eye is too small to be a self.
only the mind can be a self.
fork.reveal: he points to change: if the eye were self, you'd have to say 'my self arises and passes away', and that doesn't hold.

original.note: Pali anatta: not-self. Sanskrit anatman. tested here on thirty-six pieces of experience.

trapdoor: what you thought: not-self means you don't exist.
what it means: every piece of experience you could call 'me' arises and passes, so none is the lasting owner.
what a scholar hears: the argument works by consequence (if the eye were self, the self would arise and pass), and later Buddhist schools debated at length what the conventional person is.
